itinerary.cal: Self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead (Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness); the West Fork Buttermilk crossing runs high and log-crossing-only in early season, so most parties go July-September.

days.note: The West Fork Buttermilk Creek Trail #411 climbs at a mostly gentle grade to Fish Creek Pass, with a few steep, brushy sections and an unbridged creek crossing that can be swift in early season. From the pass the Southeast Ridge to Courtney's summit is only 45 minutes to an hour of easy Class 2 (brief Class 2-3 near the top) scrambling, so most parties tag the peak on the way in before dropping down into the Star Lake basin to camp.
days.title: Backpack in via Fish Creek Pass, tag the summit, camp at Star Lake

schedule.label: Leave trailhead
schedule.detail: West Fork Buttermilk Creek Trail #411, ~4,000 ft.

schedule.label: Reach Fish Creek Pass
schedule.detail: ~3,700-3,900 ft of gain on trail; watch for blowdowns and a high creek crossing early season.

schedule.label: Summit Courtney Peak
schedule.detail: Obvious NW-trending ridge from the pass, Class 2 with a short Class 2-3 step near the top.

schedule.label: Back to Fish Creek Pass, descend to camp
schedule.detail: Drop into Star Lake basin; established sites ~0.6 mi past the lake with reliable water.

schedule.label: Camp at Star Lake
schedule.detail: Larch-forest basin camp shared by parties also climbing Star and Oval Peaks.

days.objective: Reach Fish Creek Pass, scramble Courtney Peak's Southeast Ridge, then descend to camp

days.note: Reverse the route: back up to Fish Creek Pass and down the West Fork Buttermilk Trail to the car. No technical terrain, just a long descending trail day.
days.title: Hike out

itinerary.totalNote: A 2-day/1-night backpack: ~9.5 hr in (with the Courtney summit tagged en route) and ~7 hr out the next day, roughly 17 mi and 4,700 ft round trip. Strong parties can push it car-to-car in a very long single day, but most people backpack in to make it enjoyable.

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful interagency pass required at the trailhead
access.rules: Wilderness regulations: group size limited to 12 people; campfires are prohibited above 5,000 ft elevation; store food and pet food bear-resistant (hard-sided container, vehicle, or hung 10 ft clear of the ground); pack out all waste; no bikes or motorized/mechanized equipment.
access.permit: No wilderness permit is required to hike or climb in the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness itself (unlike neighboring North Cascades National Park, which does require permits); some trailheads keep a self-issue trail register for visitor-use statistics.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Methow Valley Ranger District (Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness)
access.passRequired: A Northwest Forest Pass (or an Interagency/America the Beautiful Annual, Day, Senior, Access, or Military Pass) is required to park at the West Fork Buttermilk Trailhead — it appears on the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest's official list of day-use fee sites.

overnight_permit.what: Free self-issue Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness permit
overnight_permit.where: Fill one out at the trailhead registration box. Most trailheads also need a Northwest Forest Pass to park.

waypoints.name: Hannegan Trailhead
waypoints.note: USFS trailhead at the end of Hannegan Pass Road (FR 32); Northwest Forest Pass required, and this is the standard jump-off for the Chilliwack/Picket Range approach.
waypoints.directions: From SR-542 east of Glacier, turn north onto FR-32 (Hannegan Pass Road) and follow Ruth Creek to the end of the road. Every camp beyond the pass is inside the national park, so the wilderness permit has to be picked up before you drive — there is no way to sort it out from here.

waypoints.name: Hannegan Pass
waypoints.note: Gateway from Mt. Baker Wilderness into North Cascades National Park; trail drops off the far side into the Chilliwack River drainage toward Boundary/Copper Creek Camp.
waypoints.directions: Four miles and roughly 2,000-2,500 ft of steady climbing on good trail up the Ruth Creek valley through subalpine forest and meadow. This is the easiest walking of the whole trip and the last of it that feels like a hike.

waypoints.name: Copper Creek / Boundary Camp
waypoints.note: National-park backcountry camp on the Chilliwack River Trail near the park boundary; wilderness permit required, typical first-night camp on the way to Whatcom Pass.
waypoints.directions: From the pass the trail drops off the north side into the Chilliwack River drainage, giving back most of the elevation just gained. The camp sits a few miles down near the park boundary and is the standard first night.

waypoints.name: Chilliwack River Cablecar Crossing
waypoints.note: Hand-pulled cable car is the only reliable crossing of the Chilliwack River when it's running high; awkward and exposed with a loaded pack.
waypoints.directions: Keep descending the Chilliwack River Trail down-valley. The tread is brushy near U.S. Cabin Camp, and in blowdown years the stretch beyond the crossing is an obstacle course of fallen trunks — parties have logged two hours to cover a mile and a half of it. The river is not reliably fordable, so the hand-pulled cable car is the crossing; sort out how a loaded pack rides and who pulls before anyone gets in.

waypoints.name: Whatcom Pass
waypoints.note: High pass reached via Brush Creek Trail; from here parties traverse the Whatcom Glacier east of Whatcom Peak to continue toward Perfect Pass.
waypoints.directions: Past the crossing, pick up the Brush Creek Trail and climb steadily up its valley. The tread here is in better shape than the Chilliwack — scattered blowdown rather than a wall of it — but the grade is long and sustained, and this is the biggest single climb of the trail approach. Whatcom Camp near the pass is the last established camp before the glaciers.

waypoints.name: Perfect Pass
waypoints.note: Reliable running water on open granite slabs; the last dependable water source and usual staging camp before committing to the glacier approach.
waypoints.directions: Leave maintained trail at Whatcom Camp and traverse cross-country onto the Whatcom Glacier, working around Whatcom Peak's northeast flank. Reckon on four to five hours and about 1,750 ft for a leg that covers only a couple of miles; it is continuous snow in normal conditions, so rope up, and it softens badly by afternoon.

waypoints.name: West Challenger Notch / Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine camp
waypoints.note: Cross the high bench of the Challenger Glacier (watch for crevasses), then make one rappel down the ice- and rock-choked gully at West Challenger Notch to reach a narrow lateral-moraine camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier's south edge, base for the summit push.
waypoints.directions: From the pass climb firm snow to rock outcrops, then traverse steep slopes west onto the Challenger Glacier and climb it roped to the high bench near 8,100 ft, passing Solar Pass. Getting off the notch means one awkward rappel down a gully choked with rock and ice; soft snow below leads to the moraine. This is a full day on its own — the glacier alone has taken parties eight hours — and fog is common enough up here that the return legs should be on GPS before you commit.

waypoints.name: Crooked Thumb Peak
waypoints.note: True summit gained via the south ridge and a 5.8+ (or 5.2/A1) headwall; descend by reversing the ridge to the north-ridge notch for two rappels off a rock horn.
waypoints.directions: Cross the glacier from camp to the foot of the northwest couloir and climb it: 40-45 degrees of snow, usually simul-climbed on pickets or flukes, and three to four hours of it. Above the couloir a narrow snow-and-rock gully gains the north ridge, then an exposed traverse around a line of pinnacles on loose Class 4-5 ledges leads to the headwall — a short, near-vertical crack at 5.8+ (or 5.2/A1). Ledges on the upper west face above it lead onto the south summit ridge. Treat every hold on the ridge as suspect and budget hard for the descent, because parties routinely run out of daylight here and end up bivouacking.
